title: One server is not enough
body: A single server handles 300 requests per second. Peak traffic is 900. You can make the server bigger (vertical scaling), but a machine has a ceiling and one failure takes everything down. Adding more identical servers (horizontal scaling) removes the ceiling, if the rest of the system can keep up.

title: Put a load balancer in front
body: Users send requests to one address, the load balancer. It forwards each request to one of several servers. The users do not know how many servers exist, and a server can be added or removed without changing the address they use.

title: Pick a server for each request
body: **Round robin** sends requests to servers in turn. It is simple and works when requests take similar time. **Least connections** sends each request to the server with the fewest open connections. It works better when some requests are much slower than others.

title: Keep servers stateless
body: If a user's shopping cart lives only in Server 2's memory, a request sent to Server 1 finds no cart. Store the cart in a shared database or a shared session store that every server can read. Then any server can answer any request.

title: Remove a broken server
body: The load balancer calls each server's health check every few seconds. A server that does not answer OK is taken out of rotation. A short interval finds failures faster but adds checking load; a long one sends more requests to a dead server first.

title: Check the next bottleneck
body: The servers now share the load, but every server still writes to one database. Scaling out moved the limit; it did not remove it. The next design step is to look at the database, which is the topic of Level 31.
